warmup.q: A program saves a payment by calling write on a file. The call returns with no error, and one millisecond later the computer loses power. Is the payment on the drive?
options: Yes: write returned with no error, so the bytes are in the file
Only if the program had also closed the file before the power failed
Not for sure: write copied the bytes into memory that the operating system manages, and only a separate call, which the program never made, waits for the drive
Yes, because a modern drive (an SSD) has no moving parts and stores data at once
warmup.why: When write returns, the bytes sit in the page cache, a copy of file data that the operating system keeps in memory. It copies them to the drive later, often seconds later. In Java the call that waits for the drive is FileChannel.force(), which uses fsync underneath: it returns only when the drive reports the data stored. Closing the file is the tempting answer, but closing doesn't wait for the drive either. It only says the program is done with the file. And an SSD is fast, but nothing reaches it until the operating system sends it there.

sections.h: Saving one payment, and when it's really on the drive
sections.html:
Let's set up the smallest program that could record card payments. When you tap your card, the reader asks your bank whether the card can pay. The bank's yes is called an authorization. Our program stores it under a key, a name to look it up by, such as auth:9001 for payment 9001, with the status AUTHORIZED. Later, when the money really moves to the shop, the status becomes CAPTURED. A payment must survive a crash, so the program adds one line to the end of a file, then replies OK to the card reader with Response.ok():

channel.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("auth:9001=AUTHORIZED\n".encodeToByteArray()))
return Response.ok()

A few words first. A byte is the smallest piece of data a computer stores: room for one letter, or a number from 0 to 255. A file is a named row of bytes kept on a drive, usually an SSD (a solid-state drive, the chip-based storage inside a laptop). The drive keeps its bytes when the power goes off. The computer's memory, its RAM, is far faster, and loses everything. channel is a FileChannel, Java's handle on one open file, and write adds the line's bytes at the end.

That write returns within microseconds (millionths of a second), and it isn't safe. The operating system is the program that runs all the others and manages the hardware, and its core is called the kernel. The kernel keeps a copy of file data in RAM, in fixed-size blocks called pages, and write only changes that copy. This copy is the page cache. (The page cache, writeback and fsync, lesson 9 of the Operating systems track, opens it up.) The kernel copies changed pages to the drive later, usually within seconds. If the power fails first, the payment is gone, and the card reader was already told OK. That's the café from the opening.

So version 2 asks the kernel to wait for the drive. In Java that's FileChannel.force. On Linux, the operating system most servers run, force(false) calls fdatasync and force(true) calls fsync. Both are system calls, requests a program makes to the kernel. Both wait until the drive reports the data stored (fdatasync can skip saving details about the file, such as the time it last changed). On macOS the JDK, Java's standard toolkit, calls fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC), which also makes the drive empty its own small memory of pending writes. A write is durable once force has returned: a power cut can no longer lose it.

Version 2 is correct, and slow. The demo for this section adds 1,000 records of 100 bytes to a file three ways. On a MacBook with an Apple chip it printed:

write only              1,000 records in      7.0 ms  =    141,893 records/s
force every record      1,000 records in   4324.6 ms  =        231 records/s
force every 50          1,000 records in    102.2 ms  =      9,782 records/s

Each force waits about 4.3 ms (thousandths of a second). So one thread, one path of work through a program, can make at most about 230 records a second durable, 600 times fewer than it can write. A busy payments program that takes 2,000 card payments a second can't wait 4 ms for each one in turn.

Version 3 keeps the rule and shares the cost. One force makes durable every byte written before it. So let several payments write, force once, then reply to all of them. Forcing once per 50 records needs 20 forces instead of 1,000, and reaches about 10,000 records a second. This is group commit. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, does it too: one force of its log can make many payments durable at once.

A reply tells the card reader the payment is safe. Force before you reply.

Two facts about the hardware sit under these numbers. The kernel and the drive never move single bytes; they move whole pages. getconf PAGESIZE prints 16384 on a Mac with an Apple chip, and 4096 in the Linux machine where this course runs PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL itself reads and writes its tables in pages of 8 KB (8,192 bytes). And adding to the end is the cheapest write there is. Every record goes after the last one, so the drive gets one steady stream and never has to change bytes it already holds.

That gives the picture for the whole lesson, in the figure. The store is one file that only grows at the end, forced before every reply. Beside it sits a map in the JVM heap, the memory where Java and Kotlin programs keep their objects (the JVM is the program that runs their code). The map remembers where each key's newest value sits in the file. The file is the truth; the map lives in RAM, so after a crash the store rebuilds it from the file.

Every database from the Data models track ends up as bytes in files like this one. The part of a database that puts the bytes there and finds them again is its storage engine. This track builds one, from this single file up to pages, indexes and crash recovery, and then turns those bytes into answers to questions. Next, we'll build the map, and find a payment again without reading the whole file.

try.title: Time write against force
steps: Predict: if one force takes about 4 ms, how long do 1,000 forced records take?
From the labs folder of the course, run the demo with the command below. Gradle, the build tool the labs use, compiles it and runs it.
Change val batch = 50 to 10, run it again, then try 200. Watch the third line.

Optional, PostgreSQL's own measurement: Docker is a program that runs other programs in containers, and on a Mac it runs them inside a small Linux computer simulated in software, a virtual machine (VM). Start the database there with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, then run docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec -u postgres db pg_test_fsync -s 2 -f /tmp/fsync.test. pg_test_fsync is a tool that comes with PostgreSQL and times force calls. Leave the database running for the next Try it.

code.title: FsyncDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.store.l01.demo import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.channels.FileChannel import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.CREATE import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.WRITE /** Appends 1,000 records of 100 bytes three ways and times each: no force, force per record, force per batch. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val records = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 1_000 val batch = 50 val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("sfz-fsync") val record = ByteArray(100) { 'x'.code.toByte() } fun run(label: String, forceEvery: Int) { val file = dir.resolve("$label.log") FileChannel.open(file, CREATE, WRITE).use { ch -> val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 1..records) { ch.write(ByteBuffer.wrap(record)) // lands in the OS page cache if (forceEvery > 0 && i % forceEvery == 0) ch.force(false) // waits for the disk } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 println("%-22s %,6d records in %8.1f ms = %,10.0f records/s".format(label, records, ms, records / (ms / 1000))) } } run("write only", 0) run("force every record", 1) run("force every $batch", batch) dir.toFile().deleteRecursively() }

try.expect: On a MacBook with an Apple chip, write only takes a few milliseconds, force every record takes about 4.2 to 4.4 seconds (about 230 records a second), and force every 50 takes 100 to 160 ms. A batch of 10 lands in between, and 200 is faster again: the cost follows the number of forces, not the number of bytes. Your numbers depend on the drive and the operating system. pg_test_fsync reported about 12,000 to 13,000 fdatasync calls a second inside the VM here. The VM's simulated disk doesn't necessarily wait for the Mac's real drive, so don't read that number as what the SSD can really do.

aside.title: If write is so unsafe, why does it return early at all?
aside.html: Because waiting for the drive on every write would slow down every program on the computer. Copying a folder, saving a photo or building code makes thousands of small writes, and most of them can be redone if a crash loses them. By holding writes in memory, the kernel answers at once and later sends many small writes to the drive as one big one. So the fast path is the default, and a program that makes promises, like our payments store, asks for force when it needs it.

sections.h: Finding a payment again: a file we only add to, and a map in memory
sections.html:
The file keeps payments safe, but how do we read auth:9001 back? The simplest answer is a scan: read the file from the start and keep the last value we see for that key. With a million records of about 40 bytes, every lookup reads 40 MB (megabytes, millions of bytes). Even from the page cache that takes milliseconds per lookup, and it grows with every payment.

The next idea is to update in place: give each key a fixed spot in the file and write over it. That breaks twice. Values have different lengths (PENDING, still waiting for the bank, is 7 bytes; CAPTURED is 8), so a fixed spot is either too small or wastes room. And a crash in the middle of an overwrite leaves a value that's half old and half new, with no copy of either.

A café's paper notebook shows a better way. The owner writes each sale on the next empty line, in pen, and never rubs anything out. A correction is a new line at the bottom. A slip of paper at the front lists, for each customer, the line that holds their latest entry. To look someone up, she reads the slip, then turns to one line.

Bitcask works the same way. It's a storage engine that the company Basho built in 2010 for Riak, its database. The notebook is the file, which Bitcask only ever adds to: an append-only log. Every put, the call that stores a value under a key, appends a record: a 20-byte header, then the key, then the value. The figure shows the exact layout your lab uses. The slip is a hash map in memory, called the keydir, and it's this store's index: a lookup table from a key to where its record lives. (A hash map turns each key into a number, its hash, that says where to look, so it finds a key in one step.) The keydir maps each key to where its newest value starts in the file, and how many bytes it has.

So get, the call that reads a key's value, is one map lookup and one read of exactly the value's bytes at that position, channel.read(buffer, position). A missing key costs no trip to the drive at all. The Bitcask paper says a read never needs more than one disk seek, one trip to the drive, and that holds by construction.

An overwrite never touches the old record. put("auth:9001", "CAPTURED") appends a new record and moves the keydir entry to it, and the old AUTHORIZED record stays behind as dead bytes. A delete can't erase anything either, so it appends a tombstone: a record with the key and no value (a value size of -1). The keydir drops the key. When the store later rebuilds the keydir from the file, the tombstone tells it the key is gone.

The picture breaks at the slip. Paper survives the night, but the keydir lives only in RAM, so after a crash the store rebuilds it by reading the whole file.

This design has two hard limits, and you should know them before you pick it. The keydir must hold every key in RAM: 50 million keys of 40 bytes, plus the map's own bookkeeping for each, is several gigabytes of memory. And a hash map keeps no order, so "every payment on card 4242 between 9:00 and 10:00" means checking every key. B+trees (lesson 4 of this track) and LSM trees (lesson 5) are indexes that keep their keys in order, and they exist to fix exactly that.

PostgreSQL uses the same append-first idea to keep its data safe. Before it changes a table, it appends a record that describes the change to its write-ahead log (WAL): an append-only file of changes, written ahead of the table itself. When a change is final, PostgreSQL appends a commit record that says so, and the payment is durable once the log has been forced past that record. The table's own pages are written later. Every position in the WAL is a byte offset, a count of bytes from the start of the log, called an LSN (log sequence number), and you can watch it move.

Appending and forcing keep every finished payment safe. But what about one that's half written when the power goes? Next, we'll cut the power in the middle of an append.

try.title: Watch PostgreSQL append to its log
steps: If PostgreSQL isn't running yet, start it from the labs folder with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. Then open psql, a small program that comes with PostgreSQL, where you type commands and read the answers: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.

Create a table, a named set of rows like one sheet of a spreadsheet, and insert one row: CREATE TABLE auth_log (id bigint, card text, status text); then INSERT INTO auth_log VALUES (1, 'card-4242', 'AUTHORIZED');. Here bigint is a whole number and text is a string.

Paste the block below. It notes the WAL position, inserts one row, notes the position again, and runs pg_waldump, PostgreSQL's tool for printing WAL records, on exactly the bytes in between. (\gset saves a query's answer in a psql variable, \setenv copies it to where shell commands can read it, and \! runs a shell command inside the container.)
Paste the block a second time. Soon after it starts, PostgreSQL writes a few records of its own bookkeeping, and the first run can show those too. Read the second run.

code.title: psql
code.html: SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset INSERT INTO auth_log VALUES (2, 'card-4242', 'CAPTURED'); SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS after \gset SELECT :'before' AS before, :'after' AS after, pg_wal_lsn_diff(:'after', :'before') AS bytes; \setenv B :before \setenv E :after \! pg_waldump -p /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker/pg_wal -s $B -e $E

try.expect:
The row costs 128 bytes of WAL. pg_waldump shows exactly two records:

  before   |   after   | bytes
-----------+-----------+-------
 0/22AB178 | 0/22AB1F8 |   128

rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):     82/    82, tx:        867, lsn: 0/022AB178, ... desc: INSERT off: 3, ... blk 0
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):     34/    34, tx:        867, lsn: 0/022AB1D0, ... desc: COMMIT 2026-11-07 17:54:44.732723 UTC

(output trimmed). rmgr names the part of PostgreSQL a record belongs to: Heap is the table itself, and Transaction holds the commit. That's an 82-byte INSERT record and a 34-byte COMMIT record, each padded to a multiple of 8 bytes, 88 and 40, which makes 128. LSNs are written in hexadecimal, base 16. Your LSNs and transaction numbers (tx) differ. Run the block again, and the new before equals the old after: the log is one stream with no gaps, and it only moves forward.

sections.h: Pulling the plug: a torn last record, and the checksum that finds it
sections.html:
Now cut the power. A crash can stop an append halfway, so the file may end with part of a record. That's a torn write. Every earlier record was forced before its put returned, so the damage can only be in the last record: the torn tail. On restart the keydir is empty, and the store rebuilds it by reading the file record by record from offset 0, its first byte. The hard part is knowing where the good records stop.

Version 1 trusts the header. Read 20 bytes, take the key and value sizes from them, read that many bytes, and repeat to the end of the file. It breaks at once. If the crash cut the last record after 13 bytes, there isn't even a whole header. Worse, a half-written header can hold any bytes at all, such as a key size of 2,147,483,647. The scan would then try to set aside 2 GB (about 2 billion bytes) of memory to read it.

Version 2 checks the sizes. It stops if fewer than 20 bytes are left, if a size is negative, or if the record claims more bytes than the file has. That catches every record that was cut short. It still believes bytes that are there but wrong. A crash can leave zeros at the end of a file, and a damaged spot on the drive can change a byte inside a value without touching the sizes.

Version 3 adds a checksum: a number worked out from a record's bytes and stored with it, so a reader can work it out again and compare. When the store writes a record, it computes a CRC-32C, a checksum of every byte after the CRC field. It's a 32-bit number, made of 32 ones and zeros, so it has about 4 billion possible values. It stores it in the record's first 4 bytes. Changing any single byte always changes the CRC, and random damage slips past it only about once in four billion tries. The scan works it out again, so the full check for each record is:

  1. If fewer than 20 bytes are left, the header is torn. Stop.
  2. Read the header. If a size is impossible (negative, or longer than what's left of the file), stop.
  3. Read the whole record and compute its CRC-32C. If it doesn't match the stored one, stop.
  4. Otherwise apply it to the keydir (a tombstone removes the key) and move on.

Where the scan stops, the store truncates the file: it cuts it back to the end of the last good record. This step is easy to forget. Without it, the next append lands after the garbage, the next restart stops at the garbage again, and every record written in between disappears.

Throwing the torn record away loses nothing anyone was promised. Its put never returned, so the card reader was never told OK. The reader sees a timeout or an error and tries again. With every try it sends the same idempotency key, a unique name for this one payment, so the program can tell a repeat from a new payment and records it once. This is the payoff of "force, then reply". A crash can lose a payment the reader knows has failed, never one it was told had gone through.

PostgreSQL ends its crash recovery the same way. Every WAL record carries a CRC-32C. After a crash, the server replays WAL records: it applies their changes to the tables again. It starts from its last checkpoint, a recent point by which all earlier changes had reached the table files. It goes on until a record fails its checks, and that failure is how it finds the end of the log. The stepper walks through the lab's version, and the Try it makes PostgreSQL do it for real.

The store now survives a crash with nothing lost that was promised, but its file never shrinks. Next, we'll clean it up without risking a single record.

try.title: Pull the plug on PostgreSQL
steps: From the labs folder, with PostgreSQL still running from the previous Try it, add 1,000 rows and note the count: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -c "INSERT INTO auth_log SELECT g, 'card-' || g, 'AUTHORIZED' FROM generate_series(3, 1002) g;" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM auth_log;". generate_series(3, 1002) makes the numbers 3 to 1,002, one row each.

Stop the server the way a power cut would, with no chance to finish cleanly, then start it again (the first two commands below). SIGKILL is a signal, a message from the kernel, that ends a program on the spot.
Read the recovery lines in the server's log, and count the rows again.
When you're done with this lesson, stop and delete the database with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

code.title: terminal, in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml kill -s SIGKILL db docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait docker compose -f env/postgres.yml logs db | grep -E 'not properly|redo (starts|done)|invalid' docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -c "SELECT count(*) FROM auth_log;"

try.expect:
The log shows a crash recovery that ends at the first bad record:

LOG:  database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress
LOG:  redo starts at 0/21DFD80
LOG:  invalid record length at 0/221EE20: expected at least 24, got 0
LOG:  redo done at 0/221EDF8 ...

(timestamps trimmed). Redo is PostgreSQL's word for replaying the log. The invalid record line isn't an error: it's the scan reaching bytes that aren't a whole record, exactly like the lab's torn tail. On another run it said invalid magic number 0000 in WAL segment ..., because the log ended where one of its pages ended. The count is the same as before the kill, because every committed row was in the WAL before its COMMIT returned.

sections.h: The file only grows: merging away dead records
sections.html:
Look at the file after a busy day. In the lab's merge test, ten card balances updated 100 times each leave 1,000 records: about 36 KB (kilobytes, thousands of bytes) of file for 370 bytes of live data. Every overwrite and every tombstone added bytes, and the dead ones stay forever. File size divided by live data is the space amplification, here about 100.

The first fix that comes to mind is to tidy the file in place, sliding live records down over dead ones. A crash halfway through would destroy records that haven't been moved yet, so that's out.

The safe fix is a merge (other systems call it compaction). It's what the café owner does when the notebook fills up: she copies the latest line for each customer into a new notebook, then throws the old one away. In code, the store reads the keydir, writes one record per live key into a new file, forces the new file, then renames it over the old one. A rename on one drive is atomic, which means all or nothing: after a crash you find either the old file or the new one, never half of each. The store swaps in a keydir with the new offsets, and the dead records are gone, tombstones included.

Real Bitcask merges without stopping writers. It closes the file it's writing once it reaches a size limit and starts a new one, so older files never change again. A merge runs in the background and reads only those closed files. Next to each merged file, it writes a hint file: only keys and positions, no values. On restart, reading the hint files rebuilds the keydir without reading every value. Your lab keeps one file and merges it whole, which is enough to see the mechanism. With one file, a tombstone can be dropped at once. With many files, it must stay until every older file that holds that key has been merged, or the old value would come back.

Merging costs writes. A live value is written once by its put, and again by every merge that copies it. Bytes written to the drive divided by bytes the program asked to write is the write amplification. Every design that only appends trades it against space. Merge often and the file stays small, but the drive writes more; merge rarely and the reverse. RocksDB is a storage engine that Facebook started and many databases now build on. Its documentation says its default way of merging, leveled compaction, often has write amplification above 10. Lesson 5 of this track measures it.

That's where today's design stops. It needs every key in memory, it can't list keys in order, and it pays for its cheap appends with merges. It belongs to the first of the two families of storage engines in this track: log-structured ones, built on a log that they only ever append to and clean up later. The other family keeps data in fixed-size pages and writes over them where they lie. The next lesson starts that family, and lessons 4 and 5 put the two side by side.

opening:
Picture a café. You tap your card to pay for a coffee, the reader beeps, and its screen says Approved. Behind that beep, a program saved a line about your payment in a file, then told the reader yes.

A second later, the computer running that program loses power. When it starts again, your payment isn't in the file. The reader said yes, and the program has no record you paid.

The program did save it, as far as it could tell. It called write, the function that adds bytes to a file, and write returned with no error. Careful programmers fall into this trap, because tests don't pull the plug.

Triples, Datalog and GraphQL, the last lesson of the Data models track, closed a tour of ways to shape data. It left one question open: how do the bytes reach a drive and stay there? In this lesson, we'll build the smallest store that could work, time a safe write, cut the power during one, and bring the store back. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a card reader that said Approved for a payment the program then lost. The file was fine; the bytes had never left memory. One call, force before the reply, closes that gap, and group commit shares its 4 ms among many payments.

On a Mac or Linux computer, open a terminal and run getconf PAGESIZE. That's the size of the blocks your operating system moves between memory and the drive. And in any program that saves something and then says OK, look for the force between the two.

Next, we'll give the engine a table too big for memory, and find out why databases cut their files into pages of exactly 8 KB.

compare.title: Replying too early vs replying after force

a.label: Too early
a.title: loses payments it already approved
a.html: fun capture(req: CaptureRequest): Response { channel.write(Record.encode(req.key, req.body)) return Response.ok() // in RAM only: a power cut loses it }

b.label: After force
b.title: safe before the reply
b.html: fun capture(req: CaptureRequest): Response { channel.write(Record.encode(req.key, req.body)) channel.force(false) // fdatasync: wait for the drive return Response.ok() // now a crash cannot lose it }

compare.note: The two functions differ by one line, and by about 4 ms on a MacBook. The first one passes every test you'll write, and loses payments it already approved when the computer dies. If the 4 ms hurts, share it: let several requests write, force once, then reply to all of them.

worked.title: Walk a recovery scan over a torn file

steps.say: After a crash, data.log is 113 bytes long, and the keydir is empty. Start the scan at offset 0 and keep two numbers: pos, where the next record should start, and size, the length of the file.
steps.code:
size = 113, pos = 0
record length = 20 (header) + ksz + max(vsz, 0)

steps.say: Check the header at 0. At least 20 bytes are left, so read it: the key size ksz = 6 and the value size vsz = 7, so the record is 33 bytes long, and it fits in the file. Read all 33 bytes, compute the CRC-32C over bytes 4 to 32, and compare it with the first 4 bytes. It matches, so apply the record and move on.
steps.code: // 1. enough bytes for a header? if (size - pos < Record.HEADER_SIZE) stop() // 2. sizes possible and inside the file? if (ksz < 0 || vsz < Record.TOMBSTONE || pos + Record.length(ksz, vsz) > size) stop() // 3. CRC over everything after the crc field if (Record.crc(bytes, Record.TSTAMP_AT, len - Record.TSTAMP_AT) != storedCrc) stop()

steps.say: Repeat at 33 (auth:2, 33 bytes) and at 66 (auth:1 again, 34 bytes). The second auth:1 record replaces the first in the keydir, because the scan applies records in file order, and the later one is newer.
steps.code:
pos = 0    auth:1 -> value at 26, 7 bytes
pos = 33   auth:2 -> value at 59, 7 bytes
pos = 66   auth:1 -> value at 92, 8 bytes   (replaces the entry above)
pos = 100

steps.say: At 100, only 13 bytes are left. Check 1 fails, so the scan stops. Truncate the file to 100 bytes and set end = 100. If instead all 34 bytes had been there but one byte of the value had changed, checks 1 and 2 would pass, and check 3 would stop the scan at the same place.
steps.code: channel.truncate(100) channel.force(true) end = 100

lab.title: Build a store that only appends, and survives a torn tail
steps: Read LogFormat.kt. It's complete: Record.encode builds a record, Record.crc computes a CRC-32C, and the *_AT constants say where each header field starts.
Run the tests once. All 12 fail, because open calls recover, which is still a TODO.

Write put: append Record.encode(key, value) at end with the writeFully helper, call channel.force(false), then point the keydir at the value (end + HEADER_SIZE plus the key's length in bytes) and move end on. Write delete the same way, with a tombstone.
Write get: one keydir lookup, then one readFully of valueSize bytes at valuePos.
Write recover with the three checks from the worked example, then truncate the file at the first bad record. The torn-tail test cuts the last record at every possible byte, so every check gets used.
Write merge. Run the tests until all 12 pass.
hints: The tests use a channel that counts calls. If "get does exactly one read" fails, you're probably reading the header before the value. The keydir already knows where the value starts and how long it is.
If "put and delete force the file" fails, the last thing put does to the channel must be force. Update the keydir after the force, not before.
Read header fields at fixed positions, such as header.getInt(Record.KEY_SIZE_AT), so the buffer's current position doesn't matter.
In merge, read each live value from the old channel before you close it. Then call Files.move(tmp, path, ATOMIC_MOVE, REPLACE_EXISTING) and reopen with channels.open(path).

drill.title: Write a safe append from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write fun append(ch: FileChannel, rec: ByteBuffer, at: Long): Long. It writes the whole record at offset at, makes it durable, and returns the offset where the next record goes. Then write, as comments, the three checks recovery makes on each record before it trusts it.

answer.html: fun append(ch: FileChannel, rec: ByteBuffer, at: Long): Long { var pos = at while (rec.hasRemaining()) pos += ch.write(rec, pos) // positional writes until it is all out ch.force(false) // fdatasync: only now may the caller reply OK return pos } // recovery, for each record starting at pos: // 1. at least HEADER_SIZE bytes left, or the header is torn // 2. ksz >= 0, vsz >= -1, and pos + record length <= file size // 3. the CRC-32C of the bytes after the crc field equals the stored crc // the first record that fails ends the log: truncate the file there

recap: write puts bytes in the kernel's page cache, in RAM. Only force (fsync on Linux, F_FULLFSYNC on macOS) waits for the drive, so reply OK only after it returns.
A force costs milliseconds, about 4 ms on a MacBook. Appending to one file and sharing one force among many writes (group commit) makes safety affordable.
Bitcask appends every put and delete to one file and keeps a keydir in RAM, so a lookup is one map lookup and one read at a known position.
A crash can only tear the last record. Recovery scans from the start, checks each record's sizes and CRC, stops at the first bad one and truncates the file there.
Overwrites and tombstones pile up. A merge copies the live records into a new file and renames it into place, paying for the space it saves with extra writes.
The limit: the keydir must hold every key in RAM and keeps no order, so a range of keys means checking all of them. Indexes that keep keys in order, B+trees and LSM trees, come later in this track.

explain.prompt: A friend is writing a small program that keeps a log of events in a file. They say: "The write call returns success, so after a crash we can't lose an event we've told someone about." Explain what can still go wrong, and what the program must do when it writes and when it restarts.
explain.answer: A successful write only means the operating system has the bytes in its page cache, in memory. If the computer loses power before the bytes reach the drive, events you already confirmed disappear. So the program must call force (fsync) before it tells anyone the event is saved. To keep that affordable, it can let several events write and then force once for all of them. A crash can also leave the last record half written. So on restart the program reads the file from the start, checks each record's sizes and checksum, stops at the first record that fails, and cuts the file off there. Dropping that record is safe, because nobody was told it was saved. Cutting the file matters too: otherwise new records land behind the garbage, and the next restart would stop at the garbage and lose them.

deeper.html:
Five details that matter once a store like this runs for real.

The folder needs a force too. A merge creates a file and renames it. Forcing the file makes its contents durable, but the rename is recorded in the folder (the directory), which the file system keeps as a separate file. On Linux you open the directory itself and fsync it, or a crash right after the rename can bring back the old name. The JDK lets you open a directory as a read-only FileChannel and force it on Linux and macOS. That doesn't work on every operating system, which is one reason the lab skips it.

Damage in the middle is a different failure. The lab stops at the first bad record, wherever it is. At the tail that's right. A bad record in the middle of a forced file means the drive or the file system damaged data later, and stopping there throws away good records behind it. Real systems react differently. PostgreSQL ends WAL replay at the first invalid record, while its data page checksums (on by default for new databases since PostgreSQL 18) report a damaged table page with an error instead of quietly dropping it. Bitcask's merge and hint files also carry CRCs, so damage is spotted, though never repaired.

Torn pages, not only torn records. A database that writes over 8 KB pages in place can be left with a page that's half old and half new after a crash, because drives write in pieces of 512 bytes or 4 KB. PostgreSQL guards against this by writing a full copy of each page into the WAL the first time the page changes after a checkpoint (full_page_writes). InnoDB, the storage engine inside the MySQL database, writes each page twice, first to a doublewrite buffer. A store that only appends sidesteps the problem: it never writes over a page that holds live data. Lesson 6 of this track comes back to torn pages.

fsync can fail quietly. In 2018 PostgreSQL developers found that Linux before version 4.13 could mark pages as written after a failed write to the drive, so a second fsync returned success for data that never arrived. PostgreSQL now stops with a PANIC when an fsync fails, and recovers from its log on restart. Do the same in your code: if force throws, don't retry and carry on.

Databases let you choose to reply early. PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit = off makes COMMIT return before its WAL record is forced. That's this lesson's early reply, made on purpose: a crash can lose the last few hundred milliseconds of commits (at most three times wal_writer_delay, which is 200 ms by default), though it never damages the database. Some data can live with that. Payments can't.
